title: The brothers come for grain (Genesis 42–44)
hook: Joseph tests them, and Judah offers himself for Benjamin

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner made governor. Your line was plan for the lean years. What did you set aside? Today closes a week that began with Jacob wrestling till daybreak. Day three hundred sixty-four.

The famine reaches Canaan. Old Jacob hears there's grain in Egypt and sends ten of his sons to buy some. Not the youngest, Benjamin. He's Rachel's last son, and Jacob won't risk him. The ten arrive and bow down, faces to the ground, before the governor of Egypt. They have no idea who he is. Years have passed. He has an Egyptian name, Egyptian clothes, an interpreter between them. But he knows them the moment they walk in. And he remembers the dreams: sheaves of grain bowing down to his. Here they are, bowing, asking for grain. What would you do with your brothers in that room?
screen: `TEN BROTHERS GO DOWN TO EGYPT.` → `THEY BOW, AND DON'T KNOW HIM.` → `HE KNOWS THEM AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Joseph doesn't reveal himself. He tests them. First, he calls them spies and holds them three days. Then he keeps one brother, Simeon, and sends the rest home: bring your youngest back, and I'll believe you. And in front of him, thinking he can't understand, they talk in their own language: we are guilty about our brother; we saw his distress when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. Joseph turns aside and weeps. Second, the hard road home. Jacob refuses to send Benjamin. Only when the grain runs out does Judah speak up: put the boy in my hands, and if I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever. Third, the trap. In Egypt, a feast, then a silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. The steward chases them down, finds it, and the governor's verdict is simple: the one with the cup becomes my slave; the rest of you can go home. Here's the door the brothers walked through once before. Years ago they let Rachel's son be carried off to Egypt and went home without him. They could do it again, and this time it would even be legal. Fourth, Judah steps forward. He tells the whole story, the old father, the lost son, how the father's life is bound up in the boy's life, and then he asks: let me stay as your slave instead of him; let the boy go home. This is the same Judah who, years ago, had the idea of selling Joseph for silver. And Matthew's Gospel traces Jesus's family through Judah, the brother who offered himself. Look back over the week: a wrestler renamed Israel, Esau running to meet him, the coat, the pit, the prison, the dreams. A family that kept breaking, and now someone stands in the gap.
screen: `SPIES! THEY CONFESS THEIR OLD GUILT.` · `JUDAH PLEDGES HIMSELF FOR THE BOY.` · `A SILVER CUP IN BENJAMIN'S SACK.` · `TAKE ME INSTEAD OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one person you could stand in for. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone carrying something heavy right now: a coworker buried in a deadline, a parent with a sick kid, a friend stuck with a hard phone call. Ask what it would look like to take their place for an hour. Cover the shift. Make the call with them. Sit in the waiting room. Don't plan anything grand. Just one offer. If you pray, you can hold that person before God, the way Judah held his brother before the governor. If you don't, just keep them in mind for a minute. The bell holds the time.
The brothers come for grain. Hungry, guilty and bowing, they're tested, until Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place. Today's word.
screen: `THE BROTHERS COME FOR GRAIN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: judah stepped forward. Today, make one real offer to take something heavy off someone else's shoulders. Day three hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Some Catholic preaching sees in Judah's offer to take Benjamin's place a picture of Christ, whom the Book of the Apocalypse calls the lion of the tribe of Juda.

fork.setup: you're one of the brothers. the governor found his cup in Benjamin's sack. he says the boy stays as a slave and the rest of you can go home in peace. what do you do?
options: go home. it's legal, and it's not your fault.
offer yourself as a slave in the boy's place.
fork.reveal: Judah steps forward, tells the whole story of the old father and the lost son, and asks to stay instead of Benjamin. the brothers who once sold Rachel's son won't leave this one.

original.note: Hebrew: grain for sale, the word Jacob uses when he hears there's grain in Egypt (Genesis 42:1–2).

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph playing games with his brothers.
what it means: a test that puts them back where they once failed, with Rachel's son in danger, and this time Judah stands in his place.
what a scholar hears: Judah's plea fills Genesis 44:18–34, and the next chapter opens with Joseph unable to hold back.

notes: Week-end look-back (days 358–364): Jacob wrestling and renamed Israel, meeting Esau, the coat, the pit, the prison, Pharaoh's dreams. Confirm the order matches the index.
'Twenty-odd years': Joseph was seventeen when sold (37:2), thirty when made governor (41:46), and seven years of plenty followed, so roughly twenty-one or twenty-two years. Confirm the phrasing.
All speeches paraphrased (42:21, 43:9, 44:17, 44:33). Confirm against the Douay-Rheims.
'One of the longest speeches in Genesis' (44:18–34): commonly said; confirm or soften.
Shever (grain for sale) at Genesis 42:1–2; confirm vocalization.
Judah as the tribe of Jesus (Matthew 1:2–3; Apocalypse 5:5, 'the lion of the tribe of Juda' in the DR) stated briefly; confirm.
